# Developer Style Guide

This file holds the rules specific to this repository: the terms its domain
uses, how material is divided across the documents under `docs/` and how
examples cover the surfaces the module exposes.  It sits at the path the core
project uses for the same purpose, so the two are read the same way.

The core Threeport project governs everything else.  Its own
`docs/dev/style-guide.md` is authoritative for Go code, imports, naming and
code comments.  The prose in this repository follows Google developer
documentation style, with these defaults: address the reader as "you", wrap
prose at 80 columns, two spaces after a sentence, use the serial comma, and use
no dash other than a plain hyphen.  Nothing here contradicts the core style
guide.

## Terminology

Record the terms this module's domain uses, one bullet each, saying which word
wins and which near-synonyms are banned.  A term settled here stops being
re-argued in every review.  The rules below hold for every module.

* A config object that creates a definition and its instance together is a
  defined instance.  Do not call it a fused config, a fusion or a combined
  config.
* Name examples after the work rather than after whatever was happening the day
  they were written.  Use sequential numbering such as `demo-01`, never a name
  derived from personal context.
* Use addresses and hostnames reserved for documentation in examples, such as
  `203.0.113.10` and `example.com`.

## Document Scope

The pages below sit under `docs/`, alongside the `dev/` directory this file is
in.  Add a bullet for each page this module carries.

* `ARCHITECTURE.md` stays high level: object model, relationships and
  lifecycle.  Keep API-usage detail out of it, including field validation,
  config examples and immutability rules.  Keep provider specifics out of it
  entirely, down to field names, since a provider-shaped field name there
  forces a rewrite the first time a second provider ships.
* `deployment.md` carries the usage documentation.  Config examples, required
  fields, validation rules and end-to-end walkthroughs live there.
* Keep the table of contents in sync with the headings, including the
  duplicate-heading anchor suffixes such as `#implementation-steps-1`.

## Examples and Surfaces

A module object is reachable three ways, so a guide that claims all three shows
all three.

* When a guide states that an operation can be driven three ways, show all
  three for every step: the `tptctl` command, the Go client call and the REST
  request.  A reader who picked the REST path should never have to translate a
  CLI example.
* Where one CLI command maps to more than one API call, say so once at the top
  rather than repeating the caveat at every step.
* Never show a credential value inline in a config example.  Configs take a
  file path, so show the `*File` form with a path, plus a shell recipe that
  writes the credential to that file first.
* REST examples necessarily put the raw value on the wire.  Say explicitly that
  the API server encrypts it on receipt, so a reader does not conclude the
  config form and the wire form share a shape.
* Define shell variables once, in a single early block, and write later blocks
  so they can be pasted as is with no edits.
* A config file is read strictly, so a key the config object does not define is
  rejected rather than ignored.  Confirm a field exists on the config type
  before showing it in a config example, and name the surface when a field is
  reachable over Go and REST but not from a config.

## Diagrams

* Diagrams are drawio SVG exports committed under `docs/img/` and referenced
  with a relative path such as `img/DataModel.drawio.svg`.  Do not embed raster
  screenshots or link to an external drawing service.
* Follow each diagram with a numbered walkthrough whose steps correspond to the
  numbered elements in the image.
* Re-export the SVG in the same change that alters the model it depicts.  A
  diagram that disagrees with the prose beside it is worse than no diagram.
